subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 16 periods = 640 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Back to School from Holidays — Students write the names of places they visited and something special about each, then ask two or three friends the same questions and fill the table (p. 131)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook opening illustration showing Chandni, Ritika, Gurpreet, and Nayan sharing holiday stories

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites three or four volunteers to share one place they visited and one thing they noticed there — a smell, a colour, a food, a sound. Responses are collected on the board in a quick list, unordered and accepting of all answers.

Students open Textbook p. 131. Each student writes the name of one place they visited (or one they have heard about from family) and something special about it. They then move to two or three classmates and ask the same question, filling the table in the textbook.

Pairs share one similarity and one difference between the places their group recorded. The teacher collects these on the board, grouping responses loosely by land type — sandy, hilly, near water, flat — without yet naming the four landforms formally.

The class looks at the board's emerging clusters. The teacher asks: what does it tell us about India that classmates who live in the same town have visited such different places? Students note one observation in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can share, compare, and record observations about places and environments using a structured table.
periods.section_context: Holiday experiences from beach (Odisha), desert (Rajasthan), plains (Punjab), mountains (Sikkim); four narrative characters; student-drawn comparisons of visited places.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whose families travel for work or weddings — they often have vivid memories of very different landscapes. Prompt: 'What is one thing about that place that surprised you or felt different from here?' Keep the mood celebratory; accuracy matters less than engagement at this opening unit.

periods.activity_title: Picture Walk: Life on the Plains
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet — Students look at the picture and write observations about the land, activities, animals, and clothing of the people (p. 132)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture of everyday farming life in Punjab (p. 132)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to look at the textbook picture on p. 132 silently for a short moment before anyone speaks. Then: 'What is the very first thing your eye went to? Tell the person next to you.'

Students write their responses to the four observation questions on Textbook p. 132 — kind of land, activities of people, animals visible, and anything unique about the clothing. Each answer is a brief phrase or sentence, not a paragraph.
The teacher invites responses question by question, building a class list on the board. Students add anything they missed from their own written answers.

The teacher reads aloud the brief passage about the Golden Temple's langar sewa. The class discusses: what does it mean to cook and serve free meals to everyone who walks in? Have any students seen or heard of a similar tradition — a community feast, a temple prasad, a neighbourhood meal — in their own area? Students note one comparison in their notebook.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record structured picture observations across multiple categories — land, occupation, animals, and clothing — in writing.
periods.section_context: Plains of Amritsar, Punjab; farming and tractors; bullocks; Punjabi attire; Golden Temple langar sewa; makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to name specific occupations they see rather than just 'farming'. When discussing langar sewa, let students connect it to any community-feeding tradition they know from their own region — the idea of collective service is widespread across India's cultures and is worth drawing out naturally.

periods.activity_title: Food of the Plains — Ingredients and Connections
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet — Students name the most popular food in their own region and list its main ingredients (p. 133)

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the task on Textbook p. 133: each student names the most popular food in their own home or region and lists the ingredients they know. Students work individually and quietly for this opening phase.

Students share in groups of four. Each group notices: are the ingredients similar or very different? Are any ingredients grown locally? Groups make a quick tally: how many different foods did four students name?

Class discussion: the teacher connects what students shared to the Punjab section — makki (maize), mustard greens, and dairy (lassi) all grow or are produced in the fertile plains. Ask: if the land around us is different from Punjab, why might our food ingredients differ?

Students write two sentences in their notebooks connecting one ingredient from the Punjab food to its source in the land (e.g. maize grows in fertile soil; mustard is a field crop). This written connection is their closing consolidation.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect regional food ingredients to the characteristics of the land and environment where they are produced.
periods.section_context: Makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi; fertile plains of Punjab; maize and mustard as field crops; student's own regional food and ingredients.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Students from different home backgrounds may name very different foods — celebrate this variety explicitly. Ask: 'Does anyone know where the main ingredient in your food actually grows or comes from?' This bridges food to land in a personal, concrete way.

periods.activity_title: The Desert in Pictures — Observing Ritika's World
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika — Students look at the desert picture and write observations about the land, plants, dress, travel, and personal preferences (p. 135)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 135 and look at the desert picture. The teacher says nothing yet — a quiet look before any questions are posed. Then: 'Tell me one word for what you see.'

Students write responses to the five observation questions on p. 135 — kind of land, types of plants and how they differ from their own locality, uniqueness of dress, mode of travel, and personal preference. Written responses are individual.

The teacher collects responses for question 2 (plants) specifically. On the board: What do cactus, khejri, and babool have in common that helps them survive with very little water? Students reason aloud from what they have just read and observed.

Brief class share on question 5 (personal preference) — what did students find most striking in the picture? The teacher names the Jaisalmer Fort as a landmark and asks students to locate it mentally: it is made of golden sandstone — the same colour as the desert sand around it. Why might builders have used that material?

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the physical features, plant life, and human adaptations of an unfamiliar environment using structured questions.
periods.section_context: Desert landform; cactus, khejri, babool; camel as desert transport; colourful Rajasthani ghaghras, bandhini dupattas, turbans; mud houses with thatched roofs; Jaisalmer Fort.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students are from a dry or semi-arid region, invite them to name drought-resistant plants from their own area — this local knowledge sits naturally alongside the textbook examples. The question about building material (sandstone) is genuinely open; wait for student reasoning before offering any explanation.

periods.activity_title: Water in the Desert — Tankas and the Scarcity Discussion
periods.section_ref: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika — Students discuss why water is scarce in the desert (p. 138)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of tanka (underground water tank) if present in the chapter

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'If it rarely rains in the desert, where do people get water?' Students discuss in pairs, drawing on what they read in the previous unit's section. Responses are brief and unrecorded at this stage.

The teacher reads aloud the textbook passage on tankas — underground water storage tanks traditionally built under desert homes to collect and store rainwater. Students discuss on Textbook p. 138: why is water scarce in the desert? They note two reasons in their notebook.

The class connects the tanka to the folk songs and dances task on Textbook p. 137. Students share what family members have told them about folk traditions from their own region — noting the name of one song or dance form and when it is performed. The teacher affirms that many folk traditions celebrate water, harvest, or the seasons because these are at the heart of daily life.

Closing discussion: the teacher asks whether anyone in the class has seen a way of collecting or saving water at home or in the community — a pot, a rooftop tank, a well, a pond. This draws the desert water problem toward a universal theme of resourcefulness. Students write one sentence: 'People in the desert save water by ___.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how people adapt traditional practices and structures to manage a scarce natural resource in their environment.
periods.section_context: Tanka (underground water storage tank); desert rainfall scarcity; folk songs and dances from student's own region; water management as cultural practice.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The tanka is an elegant piece of traditional water harvesting — invite students to describe it in their own words before explaining it yourself. Ask: 'Why underground?' Let students reason about shade and evaporation. For the folk traditions task, students who have no family input can draw on a festival or community event they have attended themselves.

periods.activity_title: Seashore Picture Walk — Chandni's Coastal World
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students look at the coastal picture and write observations about activities, trees, fun activities they would choose, and coastal dress (p. 139)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 139 and study the coastal picture for a brief, unhurried look before anyone speaks. The teacher then asks: 'What is different about the trees you see here compared to the cactus and khejri we examined in the desert section?'

Students write responses to the four observation questions on p. 139 — activities of people, trees near the sea and how they differ from desert/plains, fun activities they would choose, and special features of coastal dress. Individual written work.

Class share for question 1 (activities): the teacher builds a board list — fishing, mending nets, carrying baskets, swimming. The class discusses which of these activities is the primary livelihood and why the sea makes that possible.

The teacher introduces the Shree Jagannath Temple and Rath Yatra briefly — the giant chariot festival of Puri — and mentions the shankh (conch shell) used in rituals. Students note one connection between the coastal environment (the sea) and a cultural practice from this region.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe, describe, and compare features of a coastal environment — its vegetation, people's activities, and cultural practices — using a picture as evidence.
periods.section_context: Puri, Odisha; beach and sea; fishing as livelihood; coastal trees vs desert plants; Sambalpuri sarees; Shree Jagannath Temple; Rath Yatra; shankh.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students list activities, push them to distinguish livelihood activities from leisure activities — this is a productive distinction that appears across landforms. If any student has attended a chariot festival or similar community procession, invite that experience into the discussion.

periods.activity_title: Marine Creatures — Matching Names to Life
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students identify sea creatures by matching their names to pictures (sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish) (p. 142)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Without opening the textbook, can anyone name a creature that lives in or near the sea?' Students call out names; the teacher lists them on the board. The class looks at how many they knew and how many are new.

Students open Textbook p. 142 and complete the identification activity — matching each of the six creature names (sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish) to its picture. Students work individually first, then check with a partner.

The teacher leads a brief inquiry: for each creature, one student shares one observable feature that helped them identify it (shell, fins, branching shape, spines). The class builds a short class list: what tells us apart — feature by feature.

Closing discussion: the teacher asks, 'Which of these creatures might be in danger if we throw plastic waste into the sea?' Students reason from what they know about the creatures and what plastic does. One student is invited to make the case; others can agree, add, or question.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe distinctive features of marine creatures using visual evidence and connect creature survival to environmental conditions.
periods.section_context: Sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish; marine biodiversity of coastal Odisha; creature identification by observable features; plastic waste and marine life.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The inquiry move from identification to feature description is the key step — do not rush from matching to discussion without pausing to ask 'how do you know?' For the plastic waste discussion, accept any reasoning that connects a creature's habitat or body to the threat; you are building environmental thinking, not testing factual knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Coastal Craft — Making a Decor Object
periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students use one coastal item (or locally available substitute) to create a decorative object — photo frame, necklace, painted pebble, mini basket, or sand art jar — and display it in the class (p. 141)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the task from Textbook p. 141 and shows the range of options — photo frame, necklace, painted pebble, mini basket, sand art jar. Students are told they may use any locally available material as a substitute for coastal items. Each student decides privately what they will make.

Students make their object, working individually but in a shared, sociable atmosphere. The teacher circulates, asking students to name one coastal connection in their creation — why this shape, why this colour, what does it remind you of from the Puri section? No student needs a seashell to complete this task; a pebble, a seed, or a leaf fragment carries the same creative intent.

Students place their finished objects on their desks for a brief class gallery walk. Each student writes one sentence on a slip of paper naming their object, the coastal item it represents or is inspired by, and one thing they learned about the coast while making it.

The teacher asks: craftspeople in coastal Odisha — makers of sand art, weavers of Sambalpuri sarees — use what the land and sea offer. What material from around our school or neighbourhood could be the starting point for a local craft? One or two students share.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent their understanding of a region's natural environment through a self-made creative object and articulate the connection between material and place.
periods.section_context: Coastal decor craft; photo frame, necklace, painted pebble, mini basket, sand art jar; sand art of Puri; Sambalpuri sarees; locally available substitute materials.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The coastal connection in the object matters more than the finish quality — a painted pebble with a wave drawn on it is fully valid. Prompt students who seem stuck: 'What colour is the sea? What shape is a wave? Can you put that in your object?' Sambalpuri weaving and Odishan sand art are worth mentioning as traditions where artisans have built entire livelihoods from what their coastal land offers.

periods.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students discuss the adverse effects of a cyclone and how communities can be better prepared for such situations (p. 143)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Has anyone seen heavy rain or strong winds damage something — a tree, a wall, a roof?' Students share briefly. The teacher introduces the word 'cyclone' and asks what students already know or imagine about it.

Students read the relevant passage on Textbook pp. 142–143 about cyclones in coastal Odisha and the government's award-winning disaster management. Class discussion of the first question: what are the adverse effects of a cyclone? Students list effects on the board — flooding, damaged homes, uprooted trees, disrupted fishing, loss of crops.

Discussion of the second question on p. 143: how can communities be better prepared? Students work in pairs for a few minutes, then share with the class. The teacher notes that Odisha's preparedness has been recognised internationally — ask students what that might mean: warning systems, safe shelters, trained volunteers, community drills.

The teacher widens the discussion: the chapter also mentions landslides in mountain regions. Ask students to name one way that being prepared for a natural hazard — any hazard — is similar regardless of which landform you live on. Students note one sentence connecting preparedness to community action.

periods.implied_lo: Students can discuss the effects of a natural hazard and describe actions that communities and governments can take to reduce harm and support recovery.
periods.section_context: Cyclones in coastal Odisha; adverse effects of cyclones; Government of Odisha disaster management; community preparedness; early warning, shelters, community response.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Keep the discussion concrete — ask students to imagine a specific action, not just name a concept. 'If you heard a cyclone was coming, what is the first thing a family should do?' grounds abstract preparedness in immediate thinking. The link to landslides at the close is a bridge — do not extend it into a full new discussion; one sentence is enough.

periods.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students look at the mountain picture and write observations about animals, dress compared to their own region, and trees (p. 145)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 145 and look at the mountain picture. The teacher asks: 'What is the first difference you notice between this picture and the desert picture we studied earlier?' Students call out responses — snow, trees, thick clothing, steep slopes.

Students write responses to the three observation questions on p. 145 — types of animals in the picture, how mountain dress differs from what people wear in their own region, and a description of the trees. Individual written work.

Class share: the teacher builds a board column for animals (yak, mountain animals) and a column for trees (oak, pine, walnut, chestnut). For each tree, ask: 'Have you seen this tree or its fruit?' Students connect oak (acorns), walnut, and chestnut to things they may have encountered as food or material.

The teacher reads briefly about the yak — its thick coat, its role as a work animal and source of milk and wool in cold mountain conditions. Ask: 'How is the yak similar in its role to the camel in the desert?' Students note one comparison sentence.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the characteristic animals, vegetation, and clothing of a mountain environment using a picture as primary evidence.
periods.section_context: Gangtok, Sikkim; yak; mountain animals; oak, pine, walnut, chestnut; bakhu, dumdyam, Gunyo cholo; snow-capped Himalayan peaks; comparison with desert camel.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The yak-camel comparison is a productive analogy — both animals are deeply adapted to their landform and both are culturally central to the people who live there. Ask students to articulate what 'adapted' means in plain words before you use the term. If any student has tasted walnut or chestnut, that sensory memory anchors the tree names beautifully.

periods.activity_title: Mountain Climate — Dress, Houses, and the Cold
periods.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students discuss how the cold climate affects the way people in mountain regions live and dress, and connect to traditional clothes in their own region (p. 147)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of traditional Sikkimese wooden house with slanting roof (if present)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'When it is very cold, what do you put on or change about your home?' Students answer from experience — extra blankets, a warmer coat, shut windows, a fire or heater. The teacher records the types of responses: clothing changes, shelter changes.

Students read the relevant passage on Textbook pp. 147–148 about mountain dress (bakhu, Gunyo cholo) and traditional wooden houses with slanting roofs in Sikkim. Discussion: why slanting roofs? Students reason about snow and rain sliding off. Discussion: why wood rather than mud or stone as the main material?

Students discuss the question on p. 147 connecting traditional clothes in their own region to local climate. In pairs: what does a person in your region wear in the coldest month of the year? Is there a traditional garment — a shawl, a particular fabric, a wrap — that has been worn for generations? Share one example with the class.

The teacher asks the question on p. 148: does your house have any feature similar to mountain houses — a slanting roof, a raised floor, shuttered windows? Students think and share. The teacher frames this as an observation: every community has designed its shelters to suit its climate, often over many generations.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect features of clothing and housing design to the climate of a region and draw parallels with practices from their own environment.
periods.section_context: Cold mountain climate; bakhu, dumdyam, Gunyo cholo; traditional wooden houses with slanting roofs in Sikkim; student's own regional traditional garments and climate-adapted house features.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The discussion of traditional garments from students' own regions is genuinely region-specific — accept any valid local example. Ask: 'Did your grandparents wear the same clothes in winter that you wear now, or has it changed?' This surfaces continuity and change in cultural practice without prescribing any single answer.

periods.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students discuss why certain trees like pine and oak grow better in the mountains, and how animals like yak survive the cold climate (p. 147)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a thinking question: 'Why can't a cactus grow on a snowy mountain, and why can't a pine tree grow in the desert?' Students reason in pairs from what they know about both environments, then share with the class.

Class discussion on Textbook p. 147 questions: why do pine and oak grow better in the mountains? Students identify the factors — cold temperature, good rainfall, sloped terrain with well-draining soil. Then: how does the yak survive cold that would harm most animals? Students name the thick coat, the strong hooves for rocky terrain, the ability to eat sparse mountain grass.

The teacher introduces Loosong and Namsoong — the Sikkimese New Year celebrations with chaam mask dance. Ask: why might a community celebrate the New Year with masks and dance? Students connect the festival to the mountain calendar — the end of the harvest or the turn of the season. The teacher notes that thukpa (noodle soup) and sel roti (ring-shaped fried bread) are traditional festival foods.

Students write three sentences in their notebooks: one about why a specific mountain tree grows there, one about one adaptation of the yak, and one connecting the Loosong or Namsoong festival to the mountain season it marks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how plants and animals are suited to a specific landform's climate and connect cultural celebrations to seasonal patterns in that environment.
periods.section_context: Oak, pine, walnut, chestnut — mountain conditions; yak adaptations (thick coat, rocky terrain hooves); Loosong and Namsoong festival; chaam mask dance; thukpa, sel roti.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The cactus-vs-pine opener is a productive thinking move because students have already studied both environments — use it to let them reason, not recall. For the festival discussion, ask whether any student's community has a celebration that marks a season, a harvest, or a change in weather; this is a near-to-far connection and very common across India.

periods.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students discuss why landslides are common in mountains during the rainy season, what can be done to keep people safe, and what communities can do for those affected (p. 148)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Has anyone seen a news report or heard from a family member about a landslide or flood that moved soil and rocks?' Students share briefly. The teacher writes 'landslide' on the board and asks students to say what they think causes one, before reading the textbook.

Students read the relevant passage on Textbook p. 148 and discuss the first question: why are landslides common in the mountains during the rainy season? The class identifies the factors — steep slopes, heavy rain loosening soil, lack of tree roots to hold the soil in place. Students note two causes in their notebooks.

Paired discussion on the second and third questions from p. 148: what can be done to keep people safe during a landslide, and what can communities do for those who lose their homes? Pairs report back; the teacher organises responses into two lists on the board — 'Before and During' and 'After'.

The teacher asks students to reflect on a value: when a disaster happens to people in another region of India, what can people in our region do? Students name one concrete action — donating supplies, sending help, raising awareness — and write it down as a personal commitment sentence.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify causes of a natural hazard, propose safety measures, and articulate how communities can support those affected by disaster.
periods.section_context: Landslides in Sikkim's mountains; rainy season; steep slopes; tree roots and soil stability; community safety measures; helping affected families; disaster solidarity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The commitment sentence at the close is a values exercise — do not grade it or read it aloud unless a student volunteers. The point is to practise the disposition of community care rather than perform it. Connect the tree-roots-and-soil-stability idea to the value of protecting forests — this arises naturally from the content and does not need to be labelled.

periods.activity_title: Drawing My Landform — People, Food, and Place
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students draw the landform around them, name the area and type of landform, and label interesting features: people, professions, food, houses, plants, and animals (p. 149)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 149 and reads the task aloud. Students are asked: 'What landform surrounds our school — flat plains, gentle hills, near a river or coast, hilly or mountainous?' The class agrees on a description together. Each student will then draw their own version.

Students draw their local landform in the space provided on Textbook p. 149 (or on drawing paper). They label: name of the area, type of landform, professions of people nearby, a food item associated with the place, the type of houses, one plant, and one animal. No drawing needs to be realistic — clarity of labelling matters more than artistic finish.

Students share their drawing with the person next to them. Each partner names one thing they see in the drawing that they had not thought to include in their own. Students may add one more label to their drawing after the exchange.

The teacher asks: 'If someone from Rajasthan or Sikkim looked at your drawing, what would surprise them most about your landform?' One or two students share. The teacher affirms that every region holds knowledge and life that is worth showing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent features of their own local environment — landform, occupations, food, housing, plants, and animals — through a labelled drawing.
periods.section_context: Student's own local landform; professions, food, houses, plants, animals of the local region; labelled annotated drawing of local environment.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: This task is personal and open-ended — affirm every student's drawing regardless of artistic quality. Students who are unsure of their 'landform type' can describe it in plain words: 'flat and near a river', 'hilly with forests'. The outsider-surprise prompt at the close builds awareness that their own familiar environment is just as distinct as the four regions in the chapter.

periods.activity_title: Comparing All Four Landforms — The Big Table
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students fill the comparative table with columns for Plains, Desert, Coastal, and Mountains across categories: trees, animals, houses, clothes, food, festivals, art forms (p. 150)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 150 and shows the blank comparative table. The class names the four columns (Plains, Desert, Coastal, Mountains) and the seven rows (trees, animals, houses, clothes, food, festivals, art forms). Each student picks the one row they feel most confident about and mentally prepares their answers before writing anything.

Students fill the entire table individually, working from what they recall from the chapter's four landform sections. They do not look back at earlier sections — this is a recall and consolidation task. If a cell is empty, they leave it and return to it.

The teacher takes one row at a time and builds the table on the board by inviting students to call out entries. For contested or empty cells, the class looks back at the relevant textbook section together. The teacher corrects and adds without singling out individual errors.

Students review their completed table and circle one cell that surprised them — a fact they had not remembered correctly or had forgotten. One or two students share their circled surprise and why it was unexpected.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically organise and compare features of multiple environments across categories using a structured table.
periods.section_context: Comparative table: Plains (Punjab), Desert (Rajasthan), Coastal (Odisha), Mountains (Sikkim); categories: trees, animals, houses, clothes, food, festivals, art forms.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: The recall-first rule is important — let students attempt from memory before checking the textbook. Gaps are informative, not failures. For the festivals and art forms rows, expect regional variation in student answers; acknowledge that what students name from their own region may also be a valid addition to any landform column.

periods.activity_title: Design Your Own Landform — Imagining, Drawing, and Defending
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students design and draw a landform combining favourite features from mountains, plains, coasts, and deserts, then discuss what made them choose each feature, how each feature benefits living beings, and what difficulties people might face (p. 151)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 151 and reads the creative challenge: design an imaginary landform by combining features from all four landforms the chapter explored. Students think silently: which one feature from each landform would they most want? They write four words — one feature each from plains, desert, coast, and mountains.

Students draw their composite imaginary landform on Textbook p. 151 or on drawing paper. As they draw, they annotate: label each borrowed feature and write the name of the landform it came from. The drawing should show at least one plant, one animal, one type of house, and one human activity.

Students write brief responses to the three reflection questions on p. 151 alongside their drawing — what made them choose each feature, how each feature benefits people, animals, or plants, and what difficulties people might face in their invented landform. These can be a few words per feature rather than full sentences.

The teacher invites three or four students to show their landform and explain one feature choice. The class listens and asks one question each — 'Would it be cold or warm there?' 'What would people eat?' This is an open, celebratory close that weaves together plains, desert, coast, and mountains as genuinely different yet equally liveable worlds.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise knowledge of multiple landforms to create, annotate, and justify a composite imaginary environment, connecting physical features to the lives of plants, animals, and people.
periods.section_context: Imaginary composite landform; features chosen from plains, desert, coastal, and mountain landforms; benefits of each feature for living beings; difficulties of living in a composite environment; student reasoning and creative expression.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Welcome unusual combinations — a desert with a river, a snowy mountain next to a beach. The reasoning behind choices matters more than geographical realism. When students present, ask: 'Would the people who live here need skills from more than one landform group?' This question draws together the whole chapter's idea that environment shapes everything about daily life.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can share, compare, and record observations about places and environments using a structured table.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Holiday experiences from beach (Odisha), desert (Rajasthan), plains (Punjab), mountains (Sikkim); four narrative characters; student-drawn comparisons of visited places.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Back to School from Holidays — Students write the names of places they visited and something special about each, then ask two or three friends the same questions and fill the table (p. 131)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students share holiday destinations, record observations in the textbook table, compare places visited by classmates, and group responses by emerging land type.

coverage_handoff.section_ref: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can record structured picture observations across multiple categories — land, occupation, animals, and clothing — in writing.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Plains of Amritsar, Punjab; farming and tractors; bullocks; Punjabi attire; Golden Temple langar sewa; makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet — Students look at the picture and write observations about the land, activities, animals, and clothing of the people (p. 132)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students study the Punjab plains picture, write structured observations across four categories, and discuss the langar sewa tradition of the Golden Temple.

coverage_handoff.section_ref: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can connect regional food ingredients to the characteristics of the land and environment where they are produced.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi; fertile plains of Punjab; maize and mustard as field crops; student's own regional food and ingredients.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet — Students name the most popular food in their own region and list its main ingredients (p. 133)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students name their own regional food and its ingredients, compare across a group of four classmates, and connect Punjab's foods to the fertile plains that produce their ingredients.

coverage_handoff.section_ref: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the physical features, plant life, and human adaptations of an unfamiliar environment using structured questions.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Desert landform; cactus, khejri, babool; camel as desert transport; colourful Rajasthani ghaghras, bandhini dupattas, turbans; mud houses with thatched roofs; Jaisalmer Fort.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika — Students look at the desert picture and write observations about the land, plants, dress, travel, and personal preferences (p. 135)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe the desert village picture, write structured responses across five categories, reason about drought-resistant plants, and discuss why Jaisalmer Fort was built from golden sandstone.

coverage_handoff.section_ref: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain how people adapt traditional practices and structures to manage a scarce natural resource in their environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Tanka (underground water storage tank); desert rainfall scarcity; folk songs and dances from student's own region; water management as cultural practice.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika — Students discuss why water is scarce in the desert (p. 138)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss why water is scarce in the desert, learn about tankas as traditional water storage solutions, share folk traditions from their own regions, and connect water scarcity to universal resourcefulness.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can observe, describe, and compare features of a coastal environment — its vegetation, people's activities, and cultural practices — using a picture as evidence.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Puri, Odisha; beach and sea; fishing as livelihood; coastal trees vs desert plants; Sambalpuri sarees; Shree Jagannath Temple; Rath Yatra; shankh.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students look at the coastal picture and write observations about activities, trees, fun activities they would choose, and coastal dress (p. 139)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe the coastal picture, write structured responses across four categories, distinguish livelihood from leisure activities, and connect the shankh and Rath Yatra to coastal life.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe distinctive features of marine creatures using visual evidence and connect creature survival to environmental conditions.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish; marine biodiversity of coastal Odisha; creature identification by observable features; plastic waste and marine life.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students identify sea creatures by matching their names to pictures (sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish) (p. 142)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students identify six marine creatures by matching names to pictures, describe one observable feature per creature, and reason about how plastic waste threatens marine life.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can represent their understanding of a region's natural environment through a self-made creative object and articulate the connection between material and place.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Coastal decor craft; photo frame, necklace, painted pebble, mini basket, sand art jar; sand art of Puri; Sambalpuri sarees; locally available substitute materials.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students use one coastal item to create a fun decor object like a photo frame, a necklace, a painted pebble, a mini basket or a sand art jar and display their work in the class (p. 141)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students make a coastal-inspired decor object from locally available materials, conduct a gallery walk, and articulate the connection between their chosen material and the coastal environment.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can discuss the effects of a natural hazard and describe actions that communities and governments can take to reduce harm and support recovery.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Cyclones in coastal Odisha; adverse effects of cyclones; Government of Odisha disaster management; community preparedness; early warning, shelters, community response.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: On the Seashore, with Chandni — Students discuss the adverse effects of a cyclone and how communities can be better prepared for such situations (p. 143)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss the adverse effects of cyclones, examine Odisha's award-winning disaster management, propose community preparedness actions, and connect preparedness to a universal theme of community resilience.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the characteristic animals, vegetation, and clothing of a mountain environment using a picture as primary evidence.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Gangtok, Sikkim; yak; mountain animals; oak, pine, walnut, chestnut; bakhu, dumdyam, Gunyo cholo; snow-capped Himalayan peaks; comparison with desert camel.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students look at the mountain picture and write observations about animals, dress compared to their own region, and trees (p. 145)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe the mountain life picture, write structured observations about animals, clothing, and trees, and compare the yak's role in mountains to the camel's role in the desert.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can connect features of clothing and housing design to the climate of a region and draw parallels with practices from their own environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Cold mountain climate; bakhu, dumdyam, Gunyo cholo; traditional wooden houses with slanting roofs in Sikkim; student's own regional traditional garments and climate-adapted house features.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students discuss how the cold climate affects the way people in mountain regions live and dress, and connect to traditional clothes in their own region (p. 147)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss why mountain dress and wooden slanting-roof houses are suited to cold climate, connect these to climate-adapted clothing and house features in their own region, and examine continuity in traditional garments.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain how plants and animals are suited to a specific landform's climate and connect cultural celebrations to seasonal patterns in that environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Oak, pine, walnut, chestnut — mountain conditions; yak adaptations (thick coat, rocky terrain hooves); Loosong and Namsoong festival; chaam mask dance; thukpa, sel roti.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students discuss why certain trees like pine and oak grow better in the mountains, and how animals like yak survive the cold climate (p. 147)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students reason about why mountain trees and the yak are suited to cold conditions, and connect the Loosong and Namsoong festival celebrations to the mountain seasonal calendar.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify causes of a natural hazard, propose safety measures, and articulate how communities can support those affected by disaster.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Landslides in Sikkim's mountains; rainy season; steep slopes; tree roots and soil stability; community safety measures; helping affected families; disaster solidarity.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: In the Mountains, with Nayan — Students discuss why landslides are common in mountains during the rainy season, what can be done to keep people safe, and what communities can do for those affected (p. 148)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students identify causes of mountain landslides, propose before-during and after safety measures, and write a personal commitment sentence about helping communities affected by natural disasters.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can represent features of their own local environment — landform, occupations, food, housing, plants, and animals — through a labelled drawing.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Student's own local landform; professions, food, houses, plants, animals of the local region; labelled annotated drawing of local environment.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students draw the landform around them, name the area and type of landform, and label interesting features: people, professions, food, houses, plants, and animals (p. 149)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students draw and annotate their own local landform with labels for people, professions, food, houses, plants, and animals, then share with a partner and add one more label from the exchange.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can systematically organise and compare features of multiple environments across categories using a structured table.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Comparative table: Plains (Punjab), Desert (Rajasthan), Coastal (Odisha), Mountains (Sikkim); categories: trees, animals, houses, clothes, food, festivals, art forms.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students fill the comparative table with columns for Plains, Desert, Coastal, and Mountains across categories: trees, animals, houses, clothes, food, festivals, art forms (p. 150)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students fill the four-column comparative table from recall, check entries against the textbook as a class, and identify one surprising cell that revealed a gap or correction in their memory.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can synthesise knowledge of multiple landforms to create, annotate, and justify a composite imaginary environment, connecting physical features to the lives of plants, animals, and people.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Imaginary composite landform; features chosen from plains, desert, coastal, and mountain landforms; benefits of each feature for living beings; difficulties of living in a composite environment; student reasoning and creative expression.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Life in my Landform — Students design and draw a landform combining favourite features from mountains, plains, coasts, and deserts, then discuss what made them choose each feature, how each feature benefits living beings, and what difficulties people might face (p. 151)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students design and draw an imaginary composite landform, annotate borrowed features with their source landform, justify each choice in writing, and share their reasoning with the class in a celebratory close.

assessment_items.question_text: Chandni, Ritika, Gurpreet, and Nayan share their holiday experiences at the start of the chapter. Which pair correctly matches each child to the landform they visited?

options.label: A
options.text: Chandni — coastal; Ritika — desert; Gurpreet — plains; Nayan — mountains

options.label: B
options.text: Chandni — desert; Ritika — mountains; Gurpreet — coastal; Nayan — plains

options.label: C
options.text: Chandni — mountains; Ritika — plains; Gurpreet — desert; Nayan — coastal

options.label: D
options.text: Chandni — plains; Ritika — coastal; Gurpreet — mountains; Nayan — desert

assessment_items.annotation: Accept only option B. The four characters and their home or holiday landforms are established in the chapter's opening narrative and do not vary by region.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can share, compare, and record observations about places and environments using a structured table.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has scrambled the pairings — placing Chandni in the desert and Ritika in the mountains — suggesting they did not read or remember the opening narrative carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has inverted several pairings (mountains for Chandni, coastal for Nayan), indicating confusion between the four characters' regions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has placed all four characters in incorrect landforms, suggesting the opening narrative was not engaged with at the level of matching individuals to places.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the picture of life in the Punjab plains on p. 132 of your textbook. Name two activities you can see people doing, one animal you can spot, and one thing that is special about the clothing worn by people in the picture.
expected_elements: Two specific activities visible in the Punjab plains picture (e.g. farming, driving a tractor, ploughing with bullocks, carrying produce).
At least one animal from the picture (e.g. bullock, cow).
One observation about the clothing that is specific to the Punjabi attire shown (e.g. turban, colourful dupatta, traditional salwar kameez).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two activities visible in the textbook picture. Animal answers beyond bullock are acceptable if students can name something they genuinely observed. For clothing, accept any specific descriptive observation rather than a generic 'different clothes'. Regional variation note: students from Punjab may offer richer detail about the attire — this is a credit, not a problem.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record structured picture observations across multiple categories — land, occupation, animals, and clothing — in writing.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: Two activities from the Punjab plains picture — farming, tractor use, ploughing, or similar occupational activity.
One animal identified from the picture — bullock or cow at minimum.
One specific clothing observation — turban, dupatta, or traditional style of dress noted by name or description.

assessment_items.question_text: Gurpreet tells us that makki di roti and sarson da saag are popular foods in Punjab. Why do you think these foods are common in Punjab but might not be as common in a desert region like Rajasthan? Give one reason connecting the food to the land.
expected_elements: Identification of maize (makki) or mustard (sarson) as a crop that grows in fertile, well-watered plains soil.
A contrast with the desert — arid conditions, very little rain, and sandy soil that cannot support the same crops.
A connecting sentence linking available land/crops to what people eat in a region.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept reasoning that connects fertile soil and rainfall in Punjab to crop growth, even if the student does not use the word 'fertile'. A student who writes 'Punjab has good soil and enough rain so maize and mustard grow well there, but the desert is dry so these crops cannot grow' has answered fully. Regional variation note: students from agricultural regions may draw on their own crop knowledge — this is valid and creditable.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Agriculture, with Gurpreet
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect regional food ingredients to the characteristics of the land and environment where they are produced.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Named crop (maize or mustard) linked to fertile plains soil and adequate rainfall in Punjab.
Contrast with desert conditions — low rainfall, sandy/dry soil unable to support these crops.
Explicit connection between what the land produces and what people eat.

assessment_items.question_text: Cactus, khejri, and babool are plants found in the Rajasthan desert. What is the ONE feature all three plants share that helps them survive in the desert?

options.label: A
options.text: They can survive with very little water.

options.label: B
options.text: They grow only near rivers and water bodies.

options.label: C
options.text: They grow very tall and provide shade to animals below.

options.label: D
options.text: They produce large, sweet fruits that people eat daily.

assessment_items.annotation: Accept only option B. The survival of drought-resistant plants on minimal water is the chapter's explicit explanation for why these plants thrive in the desert.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the physical features, plant life, and human adaptations of an unfamiliar environment using structured questions.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused desert plant survival with the function of large trees — a misapplication of shade as the key feature, ignoring the water-scarcity context.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has invented a characteristic not associated with cactus, khejri, or babool in the chapter — likely drawing on a vague association between plants and fruit production.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has reversed the ecological reality — these are specifically plants that do NOT require rivers or water bodies, indicating a fundamental misunderstanding of drought resistance.

assessment_items.question_text: The people of the Rajasthan desert built tankas under their homes. What is a tanka, and why was it especially important in the desert?
expected_elements: A description of a tanka as an underground tank or storage structure used to collect and store rainwater.
An explanation linking its importance to the scarcity of water in the desert — very little rainfall, no nearby rivers or ponds.
Any additional observation about the tanka's design advantage — being underground keeps water cool and reduces evaporation.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any response that correctly identifies the tanka as a water storage structure and connects it to desert water scarcity. The third element (underground keeping water cool) is an extension — credit it if present but do not require it. Regional variation note: students from Rajasthan or other dry regions may know of similar local water storage structures; this enrichment is welcome.
assessment_items.chapter_section: In the Land of Endless Sand, with Ritika
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how people adapt traditional practices and structures to manage a scarce natural resource in their environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Tanka identified as an underground water tank or storage structure that collects rainwater.
Connection to desert water scarcity — infrequent rainfall and no nearby surface water sources.
(Optional extension) Underground location reduces evaporation and keeps water cool.

assessment_items.question_text: Chandni visits Puri on the coast of Odisha. Which of the following is the PRIMARY livelihood of people living in a coastal region like Puri?

options.label: A
options.text: Fishing in the sea

options.label: B
options.text: Growing wheat and maize on large farms

options.label: C
options.text: Herding yaks and collecting wool

options.label: D
options.text: Making pottery in desert villages

assessment_items.annotation: Accept only option C. The chapter explicitly identifies fishing as the primary livelihood of coastal communities in the Puri section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe, describe, and compare features of a coastal environment — its vegetation, people's activities, and cultural practices — using a picture as evidence.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused the coastal region's livelihood with the plains — applying Punjab's agricultural activities to a coastal setting.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused the coastal region with the mountain region — applying Sikkim's yak herding to a coastal context.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has invented a connection between pottery and the desert that is not supported by the chapter, and has misapplied it to the coastal region.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the marine creatures from the coastal section: sea turtle, crab, dolphin, corals, seaweed, starfish. Choose TWO of these creatures and describe ONE observable feature of each that helped you identify it.
expected_elements: Name of first creature chosen from the list of six.

One specific observable feature of the first creature (e.g. shell and flippers for sea turtle; hard shell and claws for crab; fins and streamlined body for dolphin; branching or rock-like shape for corals; leaf-like green strands for seaweed; five-pointed star shape for starfish).
Name of second creature chosen.
One specific observable feature of the second creature.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any feature that is genuinely observable and specific to the creature named. Do not credit generic answers like 'it lives in water' — the feature must distinguish the creature visually. Regional variation note: students from coastal regions may add features from personal experience; credit these if they are accurate and observable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe distinctive features of marine creatures using visual evidence and connect creature survival to environmental conditions.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: First creature named correctly from the six listed in the chapter.
One specific and visually distinctive feature of that creature (not simply 'lives in the sea').
Second creature named correctly.
One specific and visually distinctive feature of the second creature.

assessment_items.task: You have learned about the coastal region of Odisha — its beaches, sand art, and the things people find near the sea. Make a coastal-inspired object using materials available in your classroom or at home (a pebble, a leaf, a seed, paper, string — anything that is at hand). On a small piece of paper, write the name of your object, name ONE thing from the coastal region that inspired it, and write ONE sentence about what life near the sea is like.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My object is called: ___ 
It is inspired by: ___ (name something from the coastal region) 
Life near the sea: ___
format_of_output: A small handmade object displayed on the desk
A completed written slip with three fields filled
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the written slip alongside the object. The object does not need to be elaborate — a pebble with a wave drawn on it is as valid as a woven miniature basket. The coastal inspiration must be something named in the chapter (sand, sea creatures, fishing, sand art, shankh, etc.). The sentence about life near the sea must reflect chapter content, not simply say 'it is nice'. Regional variation note: students from coastal regions may draw on direct personal experience — this is fully creditable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent their understanding of a region's natural environment through a self-made creative object and articulate the connection between material and place.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate knowledge of a coastal environment into a creative object and articulate the link between that object and the region's natural or cultural features.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that the student has named a specific coastal inspiration from the chapter rather than a generic answer. The sentence about coastal life should reflect something from the Puri section — fishing, tides, sand art, marine creatures, cyclones, or cultural practices.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: object has a clear coastal connection the student can name; written slip cites a specific chapter element; life-near-sea sentence reflects actual chapter content. Weak: object is unrelated to the coast; written slip uses generic phrases ('the sea is big'); sentence is empty or copies a phrase without understanding.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students without craft materials can make a simple paper fold or a pencil drawing on a scrap — the written slip carries full assessment weight. Students who have visited a coast may offer richer personal detail; credit this.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The chapter explicitly tasks students with making a coastal decor item from locally available materials and displaying it — this item faithfully mirrors that task in an executable, single-session form.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter tells us that Odisha has won recognition for its disaster management during cyclones. Imagine a cyclone is approaching a coastal village. Write a short paragraph describing: (a) two harmful effects the cyclone could cause, and (b) two things the community or government could do BEFORE the cyclone arrives to keep people safe.
look_for: At least two specific harmful effects of a cyclone named and briefly described (e.g. flooding of homes and fields, destruction of fishing boats, uprooting of trees, damage to roads and buildings, loss of crops).

At least two concrete preparedness actions attributed to the community or government (e.g. early warning systems / alerts, building or identifying safe shelters, practising evacuation drills, securing boats, storing food and clean water, trained community volunteers).
A response that is grounded in coastal-landform context — not generic disaster advice but actions relevant to a sea-facing community.
Clear, readable writing — the paragraph does not need to be long, but it should be organised enough for the teacher to distinguish the two parts of the answer.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for responses that name two relevant harmful effects AND two specific preparedness actions in a coastal context. Partial credit for responses that address only one part or give very generic answers ('stay safe', 'don't go outside'). The award-winning status of Odisha's disaster management is a useful prompt — students who mention systematic, community-wide actions (not just individual ones) show stronger understanding.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can discuss the effects of a natural hazard and describe actions that communities and governments can take to reduce harm and support recovery.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

look_for: Two specific harmful effects of a cyclone in a coastal setting (flooding, damaged boats, destroyed homes, uprooted trees, crop loss, road damage).

Two concrete before-the-cyclone preparedness actions appropriate to a coastal community (early warning alerts, safe shelters, evacuation plans, securing boats, storing food and water, community drills).
Coastal specificity — actions are appropriate to a sea-facing village, not just generic disaster advice.
Organised paragraph that separates harmful effects from preparedness actions clearly.

assessment_items.question_text: Nayan's diary describes animals, trees, and dress in Sikkim. Which set of THREE things all belong to the mountains of Sikkim?

options.label: A
options.text: Cactus, camel, turban

options.label: B
options.text: Coconut palm, dolphin, Sambalpuri saree

options.label: C
options.text: Mustard field, bullock, Punjabi dupatta

options.label: D
options.text: Pine tree, yak, bakhu

assessment_items.annotation: Accept only option B. Pine, yak, and bakhu are all explicitly associated with the Sikkim mountain section of the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the characteristic animals, vegetation, and clothing of a mountain environment using a picture as primary evidence.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused mountain features with desert features — cactus, camel, and turban belong to the Rajasthan desert section, not to Sikkim.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused mountain features with coastal features — coconut palm, dolphin, and Sambalpuri saree belong to the Odisha coastal section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused mountain features with plains features — mustard fields, bullocks, and Punjabi dupattas belong to the Punjab plains section.

assessment_items.question_text: In Sikkim, traditional houses are built with wood and have slanting roofs. Explain why BOTH of these features — wood as the building material AND a slanting roof — are suited to the mountain climate.
expected_elements: An explanation for the use of wood — mountains have forests with plentiful timber; wood is a locally available material; it also provides insulation against cold.
An explanation for the slanting roof — rain and snow slide off easily rather than collecting and adding weight or leaking through a flat roof.
Both explanations connected to the mountain climate (cold, heavy rainfall or snowfall).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any reasoning that correctly links wood to local availability or insulation, and slanting roof to rain or snow run-off. Students from hilly or high-rainfall regions may draw on their own knowledge of slanting roofs — this is creditable. A student who explains only one of the two features receives partial credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect features of clothing and housing design to the climate of a region and draw parallels with practices from their own environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Wood as material explained by mountain forest abundance (local availability) and/or its insulating properties in cold weather.
Slanting roof explained by rain or snow sliding off rather than accumulating.
Both explanations grounded in mountain climate characteristics — cold, heavy rainfall or snowfall.

assessment_items.question_text: Loosong and Namsoong are New Year festivals celebrated in Sikkim with chaam mask dancing, thukpa, and sel roti. Write two sentences: one explaining why you think this festival might be celebrated at a particular time of year in the mountains, and one describing a festival from your own region that also marks a season or an important time of year.
expected_elements: A sentence connecting the Sikkimese New Year festival to a seasonal or agricultural moment in the mountain calendar (end of harvest, beginning of winter, turn of the year).
A named festival from the student's own region with a brief description of the time of year or occasion it marks.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: the second sentence is genuinely region-specific — accept any festival the student names from their own community, whether it marks a harvest, a season, a religious occasion, or a community event. Do not expect a single correct answer. Award full credit if both sentences are present and the first shows any reasoning connecting the festival to a mountain seasonal context.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how plants and animals are suited to a specific landform's climate and connect cultural celebrations to seasonal patterns in that environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

expected_elements: First sentence connects Loosong or Namsoong to a mountain seasonal turning point — end of harvest, onset of winter, New Year in the Sikkimese calendar.
Second sentence names a festival from the student's own region and identifies the season or occasion it marks.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter tells us that landslides are common in the mountains during the rainy season. Write a paragraph explaining: (a) two reasons why landslides happen more in the rainy season, and (b) two things people or communities can do to be better prepared for a landslide.
look_for: Two reasons for landslides in the rainy season — heavy rain loosens and saturates soil on steep slopes; water weakens the grip of soil and rocks; fewer tree roots (or deforestation) means less soil anchoring; steep mountain terrain allows rapid downward movement of soil and rock.

Two preparedness or response actions — building warning systems, identifying and moving to safe higher ground, not building on steep unstable slopes, community drills, keeping emergency supplies, helping families who lose homes.
A response that shows understanding of the mountain setting — not generic flood advice but actions suited to steep slope landslide risk.
Writing that is organised enough to distinguish the two parts of the answer.
assessment_items.annotation: Full credit for responses addressing both parts with mountain-specific reasoning. Accept any two valid causes and any two concrete actions. Credit the connection between tree roots and soil stability as a particularly strong understanding marker — it bridges the natural science and the values content of the section. Regional variation note: students from hilly or mountainous regions may add first-hand observations; credit these.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify causes of a natural hazard, propose safety measures, and articulate how communities can support those affected by disaster.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

look_for: Two specific causes of rainy-season landslides in mountains: heavy rainfall saturating soil; steep slopes; absence of tree roots to anchor soil.
Two concrete preparedness or community support actions: warning systems, evacuation to safe ground, not building on unstable slopes, emergency supplies, community help for affected families.
Mountain specificity — the causes and actions are appropriate to steep-slope landslide risk, not generic flood advice.
Organised paragraph with causes and actions distinguishable.

assessment_items.task: Draw the landform where you live. Label at least FOUR of these: the type of landform, one profession of people nearby, one food from your region, one type of house in your area, one plant that grows near you, one animal you have seen locally. Below your drawing, write one sentence: 'The most interesting thing about where I live is ___.'
assessment_items.scaffold:
Type of landform: ___ 
Labels on drawing: (at least 4 from the list above) 
My sentence: The most interesting thing about where I live is ___.
format_of_output: A labelled drawing of the local landform
A completed sentence below the drawing
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: every student's answer here is inherently regional — there is no single correct content. Assess that: (1) the landform type is named or described, (2) at least four labels are present and are genuinely local, (3) the sentence names something specific rather than a generic statement. Quality of drawing does not affect the mark — accuracy and specificity of labels and sentence matter. Students who cannot name the landform type may describe it in plain words ('flat land with fields', 'hilly with lots of trees') — accept this.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent features of their own local environment — landform, occupations, food, housing, plants, and animals — through a labelled drawing.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the chapter's landform-observation framework to their own environment and represent it through a labelled drawing — showing that they understand the connection between land and life.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that the landform type is named or adequately described, that at least four of the six label categories are present and locally specific (not generic), and that the sentence names something particular to their place.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: landform named, four or more specific local labels, sentence names a concrete local feature. Weak: labels are generic ('a tree', 'a person'), landform is unlabelled, sentence is empty or says 'it is good'.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot draw confidently may make a simple outline with clear labels — the written labels carry the assessment weight. Students who live in an urban setting may label buildings, roads, parks, and urban professions; this is valid if genuinely local.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The chapter task on p. 149 asks exactly this — draw your landform and label its features. This item mirrors that task directly.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter compares four landforms of India. Which row in the comparison table correctly matches a landform to ONE feature of the people who live there?

options.label: A
options.text: Coastal — people herd yaks for milk and wool

options.label: B
options.text: Desert — fishing is the main livelihood

options.label: C
options.text: Mountains — people wear light cotton clothes all year

options.label: D
options.text: Plains — farming is the main livelihood

assessment_items.annotation: Accept only option B. Farming as the primary livelihood of the fertile Punjab plains is a central claim of the chapter.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically organise and compare features of multiple environments across categories using a structured table.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused the desert with the coast — fishing is the livelihood of coastal communities, not desert communities where camel herding and trade are more relevant.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has reversed the mountain clothing reality — mountain people wear warm, layered clothing (like the bakhu) because of cold conditions, not light cotton.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused the coastal region with the mountains — yak herding is associated with Sikkim's mountains, not with coastal Odisha.

assessment_items.task: Design your own imaginary landform by combining ONE feature each from the plains, desert, coastal region, and mountains of India. Draw your landform and label each borrowed feature with the name of the landform it came from. Then answer in writing: (a) Why did you choose this feature? (b) How does this feature help the people, animals, or plants in your landform?
assessment_items.scaffold:
My imaginary landform has: 
- From the plains: ___ because ___ 
- From the desert: ___ because ___ 
- From the coast: ___ because ___ 
- From the mountains: ___ because ___ 
How each feature helps living beings: ___
format_of_output: A drawn and labelled imaginary composite landform
Written justifications for each of the four chosen features
assessment_items.annotation: This is a synthesis task — assess the quality of reasoning over the quality of drawing. A student who chooses 'fertile soil from the plains' and explains that it helps crops grow, or 'the sea from the coast' and explains that people can fish, has demonstrated understanding of the environment-life relationship across the chapter. Accept any combination of features as long as each is traceable to one of the four chapter landforms and the justification is chapter-grounded. Regional variation note: students may draw on their own landform as a fifth inspiration — credit this if it is explicitly labelled as their own region.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise knowledge of multiple landforms to create, annotate, and justify a composite imaginary environment, connecting physical features to the lives of plants, animals, and people.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can draw on knowledge of all four chapter landforms to make deliberate choices, name the source of each feature, and justify how that feature supports life — demonstrating synthesis-level understanding of the environment-culture relationship.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that all four landform sources are represented, that each chosen feature is named and labelled, and that the justification for each is chapter-grounded (not vague). The 'how it helps' question is the cognitive core — it requires the student to think about cause and effect between landscape and life.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: four distinct landform features chosen and labelled by source; justifications are specific and connected to chapter content (e.g. 'mountains give pine forests so people have wood to build warm houses'). Weak: features are unnamed or not traceable to a specific landform; justifications are generic ('it is good for people').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with drawing may use labelled boxes or simple outlines — the written justifications carry the primary assessment weight. Students who choose features from their own region as one of the four can receive credit if that region is identifiable as one of the chapter's landforms.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Labelled composite drawing with written justifications
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The chapter's final creative task on p. 151 asks exactly this — design and draw a composite imaginary landform and reflect on feature choices and their consequences for living beings. This item mirrors that task faithfully.
